video:video.video:title: 800.com Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: It does one thing cleanly: toll-free and vanity numbers with call tracking and routing. But it's a phone-number layer, not a full business-comms platform, so you won't get team chat, video or a contact center here. The 1,000-minute cap on Startup matters for higher call volume, and the step up to Small Business more than doubles the bill. For a business that mainly wants a professional toll-free presence and call analytics, it's straightforward and fairly priced. The 2026 AI Agents (auto-answering, appointment booking, spam filtering) are the newest piece and sit in the bundled Complete plan, so treat them as young rather than proven.

video:video.video:title: Aircall Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Two structural catches: the 3-seat minimum makes the real starting price triple the sticker, and the annual-vs-monthly gap is steep (Professional: $50 vs $70). 'Unlimited calling' covers listed regions — check yours — and AI features increasingly live in add-ons or higher tiers. It's polished and integration-rich; just price the seats you'll actually have, on the billing cycle you'll actually choose.

video:video.video:title: Answering Service Care Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Do the arithmetic before you pick a tier, because their own page does not. Starter buys the line and nothing else: at $40 plus $1.75 a minute, it stays the cheapest option only up to roughly 79 minutes a month — past that the $179 Small Business plan costs less. The same crossover logic repeats: Small Business gives way to Pro at about 188 minutes, and Pro gives way to Enterprise at about 444. Note too that Small Business is the one tier where an included minute ($1.79 each, $179 for 100) costs more than an overage minute ($1.70), so there is no saving in buying that bundle for its own sake. And the second thing to price in is the $50 start-up fee, which is easy to miss where they have put it.

video:video.video:title: Calilio Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The subscription is the platform, not the talking: numbers, minutes and SMS meter separately from a credit balance, so an active calling team's real bill sits meaningfully above the per-seat sticker — model a month of your actual call volume before comparing vendors. It's a young player in a crowded VoIP field; the price is keen, so test call quality on your real routes in the trial.

video:video.video:title: CallHippo Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: 'Unlimited calling' is unlimited to the US and Canada — international minutes meter separately, so teams calling Europe or Asia should price their real destinations first. The plan grid is busy (two suites, add-ons for the dialer and AI), which makes comparisons slippery: list the five features you actually need and find the cheapest tier that truly contains all five.

video:video.video:title: CloudTalk Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The per-seat price is only part of it — number rental, outbound minutes and the AI add-ons stack on top, so a call-heavy team's real bill runs above the plan rate. Solid CRM integrations, but model your call volume first.

video:video.video:title: Cloze Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Two things to weigh, and the first is the price itself. On the same day, the App Store listing sold this at $49, $99 and $199 a month for 250, 750 and 2,000 conversations. The vendor's own site sold it at $29 and $79, with unlimited conversations on both paid tiers. The screenshot below is that page. Two prices and two different meters for one product is not a discount you can claim, it is an inconsistency to ask about before you pay. The second is the track record, or the absence of one. The app launched 24 April 2026 and, as of 4 September 2026, carries exactly one review — five stars, left after eight days of use. So there is next to no merchant experience to lean on, and the “Built for Shopify” badge is a technical bar, not a verdict on the answers. Also note what a conversation costs when it goes wrong. An assistant wired to live inventory and order tracking is answering with your data, and the free tier's 25 conversations a month is enough to test the tone but not enough to see it handle a bad day. The 3-day trial on paid plans is short for a support tool.

video:video.video:title: CometChat Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The pricing cliff is the honest headline: from a 100-MAU free tier straight to ~$239/mo is a brutal jump for an early-stage app, and users report plan structures changing under them. Model your MAU growth curve and the overage math before you architect around it. Chat infrastructure is sticky by nature; the time to compare vendors is before launch, not after.

video:video.video:title: CrankWheel Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: It's deliberately narrow — instant, no-download screen sharing for sales calls — so it's excellent at that one job and thin everywhere else: no full video-conferencing suite, no deep collaboration or webinar tooling. Mind which plan caps what: the free plan drops to 15 sessions a month after the first fortnight and Team puts everyone on a shared pool of 100, while Solo is the one paid tier with unlimited usage. If you want an all-purpose meeting platform, this isn't it; if you want prospects to see your screen in seconds with zero friction, that focus is exactly why it works.

video:video.video:title: Fireflies.ai Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The advertised $10 and $19 are annual-billing rates; month-to-month is $18 and $29. And AI credits are capped on every tier — Pro carries the same 20 a month as the free plan, so upgrading to Pro buys recording and storage rather than more AI. If you mainly want real-time in-Zoom captioning and simple English notes, Otter is the simpler pick.

video:video.video:title: Freshworks Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Freshworks is not a product, it is nine of them behind a pricing page that contains no price. Once you find Freshdesk's own page, two things sit on top of the number. Freddy AI Copilot — the AI the marketing leads with — is $29 per agent per month extra, 53% on top of a Pro seat, and it is not sold on Growth at all. And the Freddy AI Agent that is included stops after 500 sessions; beyond that it is $49 per 100 sessions, so a busy queue turns the included allowance into a metered bill. The SAVE 20% badge on the annual toggle is really 17%. If you want support and IT and CRM, price three subscriptions, not one.

video:video.video:title: Gorgias Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
Never priced per agent is a real advantage, but it starts one tier up: the comparison table caps Starter at 3 user seats, and only Basic and above open the inbox to 500. On Basic upwards your whole team can be in there without the bill moving, which is the main reason to choose this over a per-seat helpdesk.
The cost sits on two meters instead, and both bite. Tickets beyond your allowance are $0.40 each on Starter and Basic, $0.36 on Pro and Advanced, so a bad week costs money rather than attention. And the AI agent -- the thing the homepage leads with -- is a separate $30 a month on the entry plan, which is three times the helpdesk it sits on. So the honest entry price for the product as advertised is $40, not $10.
Count a normal month's tickets and a busy month's, and price both. Then check the AI meter separately: the plan cards charge $1.50 per automated interaction past the included allowance while the comparison table on the same page says $1.00 to $0.85 depending on tier. When a vendor publishes two rates for the same meter, get the one that will be on your invoice in writing before you switch the agent on.

video:video.video:title: HelpCenter Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The free tier is the hook and the FAQ builder is the reason people stay. But the meter is tickets, not agents: Basic hands you unlimited support staff and then charges $0.16 for every ticket past fifty. At 300 tickets a month that is $45.99, against $19.99 for the Standard tier that includes them outright — so check your own ticket volume before you treat $5.99 as the price. One dependency worth knowing: translating FAQs into other languages is handed off to a separate app (LangShop), so a multilingual store is two subscriptions, not one.

video:video.video:title: Kixie Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Plan for 30-60% above the sticker: minutes, the multi-line dialer and AI human-voice-detection all bill separately, and the quarterly auto-renewing contract only allows downgrades in its final 30 days — read that clause before signing. The dialer itself is genuinely fast and CRM-native; just buy it with the full basket priced and the calendar reminder set (our Renewal Radar exists for exactly this).

video:video.video:title: KrispCall Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Same honest math as most budget VoIP: the plan buys the platform, the meter buys the conversations — per-minute and per-SMS charges land on top of every seat, so the comparison that matters is call-rate-per-country at your volume. The 100+ country number coverage is genuinely the draw; verify number availability and local regulations for your specific target countries before committing.

video:video.video:title: Lucrovox Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
The meter is AI-handled calls: Starter’s 100 calls a month is roughly three a day, so a genuinely busy shop outgrows it quickly — and the steps are steep ($199 → $499 → $999). The ‘callers can’t tell it’s AI’ claim is the vendor’s own: they offer a live demo number, so test that before you commit.
One more thing to read carefully on the sibling product's page. LucroChat's ROI calculator reports its return “Based on Growth plan ($99/mo)”, while the plan table on the same page prices Growth at $59 a month (first read 24 August 2026, unchanged when we re-read it on 15 September 2026, and still there after the vendor told us that day it had been fixed). The $99 is the higher of the two, so nobody is being lured with a low number, but a page that quotes two different prices for one plan is a page whose figures you check at checkout rather than take on trust.

video:video.video:title: NeuroAds Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
The app is ten weeks old. It launched on 5 June 2026 and, as of 19 August 2026, has six reviews — all five stars, all posted between 7 and 15 August, by merchants who had had it installed for five, eleven and thirteen days. Nothing about that is suspicious on its face; new apps have new reviews. But six enthusiastic first impressions from people two weeks in tell you the setup is smooth and tell you nothing about what happens when the bot gets a refund question wrong in month four. On the same page, Shopify Inbox is free with 5,488 reviews.
The listing contradicts itself on the trial. The summary at the top of the page promises a 30-day trial; the pricing table shows a 7-day free trial on all three paid plans. Assume seven days, because that is the number in the row you actually click, and check it in the charge screen before you rely on a month.
And look at what it asks for. This app requests names, email addresses, phone numbers and physical addresses of your customers, plus geolocation and IP, sixty days of order history, your discount codes and your store pages. That is a defensible list for a bot that tracks orders and offers codes, and it is also a lot of customer data to route through a ten-week-old company on the strength of six reviews. Read the privacy policy, and check where the conversations are stored, before you switch it on for a store with EU shoppers.

video:video.video:title: Pylon Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The per-seat sticker is the entry ticket; the AI that makes the platform sing is metered separately, so a realistic modern deployment (seats + AI agent + phone) lands well above the tier price — model your full basket. That said, its B2B-native design (Slack/Teams-first support, account-based views) is a genuine fit gap that classic ticket tools fake with workarounds.

video:video.video:title: Quo Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Call reliability is the recurring complaint — G2 logs hundreds of connection and disconnection reports, and calls get shaky the moment you're off Wi-Fi. There's also no video conferencing, no 24/7 support on lower tiers, international calling costs extra, and the CRM integrations are shallow (the HubSpot app scores ~3.3/5).

video:video.video:title: Readymode Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The per-seat price is premium, and the model rewards scale — the predictive dialer, compliance tools and supervisor monitoring earn their keep on a 5-plus-agent floor, but for one or two reps it's expensive for what a lighter dialer would do. Predictive dialing also carries compliance responsibility (TCPA and similar): the speed is only an asset if your calling practices stay compliant. For high-volume outbound teams, it's a genuine efficiency engine.

video:video.video:title: Ruby Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: You're paying premium rates for real human receptionists billed per minute — worth it when a missed call is a lost client, but expensive if your call volume is low or an AI answering service would do the job for a fraction.

video:video.video:title: Salesmessage Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Two things changed here and both cost money. First, calling now runs on the same meter as texting — 1 credit a minute, 2 a minute when forwarding — so voice minutes eat the allowance you budgeted for messages. Second, the plan ladder is a canyon: $25 to $329 a month with nothing between them, and the credits dropdown raises your allowance without adding a single seat. Size the credits, not the headcount. An MMS is 2 credits, so one picture message to 1,000 contacts is 2,000 credits — four times the entire monthly allowance on Basic. Seats and numbers bill on top of every plan beyond the first of each: a five-person team on one number is $40 a month over the sticker, and the annual headline of $21 and $277 is a per-month display of a bill charged yearly. Note what the page has stopped saying since our previous check: there is no published per-credit overage rate anymore, so what happens when you run out mid-cycle is not stated where you buy — ask before you commit. And US business texting carries a regulatory layer of its own: 10DLC registration and carrier surcharges bill separately from anything quoted here, and opt-in and opt-out handling stays your legal responsibility — the platform enables compliance, it does not absolve you.

video:video.video:title: Signal House Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
Two things are missing from a page that is otherwise unusually specific. The first is voice. The product is sold as an SMS and Voice API and the pricing page publishes no voice rate at all — nor short code pricing. If the voice half is why you are looking, you cannot budget it from public information and will have to ask.
The second is the arithmetic behind the Twilio comparison, which is the whole pitch. Take the entry rate with no minimum. Signal House is $0.0065 a segment against Twilio’s $0.0083, which reads as a 22% saving. But carrier fees are a pass-through and identical either way: add T-Mobile’s $0.0045 to both and you get $0.0110 against $0.0128 — about 14%, not 22%. Numbers narrow it further, $1.00 against $1.15. So the saving is real and it is worth having at volume, but it is a discount on the platform margin rather than on your bill, and the headline does not make that distinction. On a million segments a month that difference is roughly $1,800 a month against Twilio’s list — worth switching for, provided the voice side does not turn out to be where the money goes.
Worth noting on the other side: Signal House prints its A2P 10DLC registration fees on the pricing page, and Twilio’s equivalent page says only that fees apply and points elsewhere. Being able to see the whole bill before you sign is not nothing.

video:video.video:title: StoreFAQ Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description:
The meter is FAQ page views, and that is the thing this app exists to increase. You install it to get SEO-friendly FAQ pages that rank and get read; every read is a billable unit. The free plan stops at 100 views and Professional at 500, which a product-page FAQ on a store with any traffic burns through in days, and then it is $0.0159 a view. Unlimited views arrive only on the $49.99 tier. Success on the cheap plans costs you money, which is an odd shape for a pricing page and the first thing to model before you install.
The AI allowance is the second meter and it is tight. Twenty-five conversations for the entire life of a free account, fifty a month at $7.99, a hundred at $14.99, and $0.30 each after that. Two hundred extra conversations in a month is $60, more than the top tier costs outright, so if the chatbot is the reason you are here, price the conversations rather than the subscription and jump straight to the tier that fits.
And know the boundary of the tool. This builds FAQ content, schema and a light chat layer. It is not a helpdesk: no ticketing, no agent queues, no multichannel reporting. Anything a shopper asks that an FAQ cannot answer still lands in whatever inbox you had before.

video:video.video:title: Textline Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Two costs are easy to miss and both are monthly. The credit system has two rates: $0.03 for credits you buy deliberately and $0.04 for backup credits that fire automatically when you run out — a 33% premium for not noticing. And a $15 monthly 10DLC campaign fee appears on your bill if you use a 10DLC long code, charged by the carrier registry rather than by Textline, so no plan removes it; the same page notes that toll-free numbers carry no monthly registration fee, so the number type is the lever, not the tier. Plan prices are still not published — the page names Essentials, Pro and Enterprise and what they include, but no dollar figures.

video:video.video:title: UniTel Voice Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: It's a virtual phone layer, not a full unified-comms suite — you won't find the deep team messaging, video meetings and contact-center features pricier platforms bundle. For a solo founder or small team that just needs a professional number, auto-attendant and call routing, that focus is exactly the point; for a larger org wanting one platform for everything, it will feel thin.

video:video.video:title: Vida AI Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: This is priced for agencies and telecoms reselling AI phone agents, not for a single small business wanting one receptionist bot. Every deployment starts with a scoped pilot from $1,500, credited toward your first month, and the production price arrives as a quote afterwards — so you cannot compare it on price until you have spent money finding out. And the universal truth of voice AI: demo calls are rehearsed, your callers aren't. Pilot it on your real call types (accents, interruptions, edge requests) and measure containment rate before betting the front desk on it.

video:video.video:title: Voye Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: eSIM data pooling genuinely beats classic roaming for traveling teams, but the honest homework is coverage-and-speed on YOUR corridors: quality varies by country and local carrier partner, so pilot with two or three of your heaviest travelers before migrating everyone. And note the vendor-cited savings numbers are marketing math until your own invoice confirms them.

video:video.video:title: Wati Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The plan price is the smallest part of the bill. Growth is capped at three users and you cannot buy a fourth at any price, so growing past three people forces the jump to Pro; from there extra seats are €39 each, and €89 each on Business, on the euro storefront we have been served since August (our July dollar reading of the same two lines was $24 and $69). Automation triggers, AI co-pilot credits, the Astra AI agents, the Shopify link and every additional WhatsApp number are all separately metered, and Meta's per-conversation fees land on top of the lot. Model your real message volume and seat count before committing — that is where the money actually goes.

video:video.video:title: Weave Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Two honest cautions. The $199 starting price is a floor, not the bill: add-ons, setup and per-location fees land on top, and the full tier ladder is only shown in a demo, so get everything in writing. And it's deeply tuned for healthcare and appointment-based practices; a general small business will find much of the workflow assumes a front desk and a patient schedule.

video:video.video:title: ZenZap Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The pricing genuinely undercuts Slack — the honest question is ecosystem: team chat lives or dies on integrations and habit, and ZenZap's app catalog is a fraction of Slack's, so teams glued to hundreds of integrations will feel the gap. For WhatsApp-refugee teams that mainly need organized channels, tasks and work/life separation, the free tier is a remarkably complete landing spot.

video:video.video:title: Zendesk Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: Three separate multipliers sit on top of the number you first see. The prices shown are annual-billed — the page states a 20% annual discount and never prints the monthly rate, so budgeting month-to-month means adding roughly a quarter yourself. Copilot, the AI the product is currently sold on, is a $50 per-agent add-on that their own page restricts to Professional and higher: the $19 and $55 tiers cannot have it at any price, and on the $115 Professional seat it is a 43% uplift. And the AI agents that are included are metered by automated resolutions: past the allowance you pay per resolution, so the bill moves with how well the AI works rather than with how many people you hire. App Builder, Action Builder and Voice are metered on consumption alongside it. Price the tier you need with the add-ons you actually want switched on, because the $19 entry and a working configuration are far apart.

video:video.video:title: eDesk Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: There are two meters, and the second one is easy to miss. The per-agent price is the entry ticket, but the AI Agent charges $0.99 for every automated resolution on top. That is great when it deflects real tickets, but it is a variable line item that scales with your support volume — model it against your ticket count before assuming a flat bill. And the honest fundamental for any e-commerce helpdesk: the value is only as good as your marketplace integrations actually syncing — test Amazon/eBay/Shopify connections with your real accounts during the free trial.

video:video.video:title: respond.io Review (2026) — honest pricing & who should skip it
video:video.video:description: The entry plan is the inbox without the engine. At $79 you get shared inboxes across WhatsApp, Instagram, Messenger, SMS and live chat, and that alone solves the “five people answering from one phone” problem. But workflow automation, broadcasts, AI Agents and the API — the things most people picture when they read “omnichannel platform” — begin at $159, so the real entry price for an automated setup is double the headline. Work out which side of that line you sit on before comparing it with anything else. And note the meter: you pay per active contact per month, so cost follows how many people message you, not how many staff you add. That is kinder than per-seat pricing for a small team fielding a lot of chats, and harsher if you have a big list you talk to often.
